    <article>
        <header class="article-header">
            <div class="article-category"><i class="fas fa-cat"></i> Mass Exploitation Campaign</div>
            <h1>Operation PCPcat: 59,000 Next.js Servers Hacked in 48 Hours</h1>
            <p class="article-excerpt">A massive credential-theft campaign dubbed "PCPcat" compromised 59,128
                Next.js and React servers in under 48 hours. But the real lesson isn't about patching—it's about why
                your "frontend" framework is now the most dangerous part of your infrastructure.</p>
            <div class="article-meta">
                <span><i class="far fa-calendar-alt"></i> Attack: December 2025</span>
                <span><i class="fas fa-clock"></i> Published: Dec 25, 2025</span>
                <span><i class="fas fa-book-open"></i> 18 min read</span>
            </div>
        </header>

        <img src="/images/articles/operation-pcpcat-2025.png" alt="Operation PCPcat Next.js React Hack"
            class="featured-image" loading="lazy">

        <div class="warning-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> URGENT - Mass Exploitation:</strong> Operation
            PCPcat achieved a 64.6% success rate across 91,505 scanned targets. If you run Next.js or React with
            server-side rendering (SSR), assume you were scanned. Check for CVE-2025-29927 and CVE-2025-66478
            immediately.
        </div>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-lightbulb"></i> The Uncomfortable Truth About "Frontend" Frameworks</h2>

        <p>Let me start with a controversial statement: <strong>Next.js and React are not frontend frameworks
                anymore.</strong> They haven't been for years. And this fundamental misunderstanding is why 59,128
            servers just got pwned in 48 hours.</p>

        <p>When developers think "React," they think browser. They think client-side rendering. They think "it's
            just JavaScript in the browser, what's the risk?" But modern React with Next.js is a full-stack Node.js
            server that:</p>

        <ul>
            <li>Executes code on the server before sending HTML to the browser</li>
            <li>Has direct access to environment variables containing production secrets</li>
            <li>Can read and write to databases, APIs, and cloud infrastructure</li>
            <li>Often runs with the same privileges as your backend services</li>
        </ul>

        <p>Operation PCPcat didn't hack "websites." It hacked <strong>servers</strong>. And those servers had the
            keys to everything.</p>

        <div class="blue-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-brain"></i> The Mental Model Problem:</strong> Security teams often treat
            Next.js deployments as "frontend" and apply weaker controls. Developers create `.env` files with
            production AWS keys because "it's just for the build." This cognitive gap between "React = browser" and
            "Next.js = server" is exactly what attackers exploit.
        </div>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-file-alt"></i> What Is Operation PCPcat?</h2>

        <p>Operation PCPcat is a large-scale, automated credential-theft campaign that targeted Next.js and React
            applications with server-side rendering capabilities. The campaign was named after the distinct
            cat-themed motifs found in the attack infrastructure.</p>

        <div class="stat-grid">
            <div class="stat-card">
                <span class="stat-value">59,128</span>
                <span class="stat-label">Servers Compromised</span>
            </div>
            <div class="stat-card">
                <span class="stat-value">48 hrs</span>
                <span class="stat-label">Attack Duration</span>
            </div>
            <div class="stat-card">
                <span class="stat-value">64.6%</span>
                <span class="stat-label">Success Rate</span>
            </div>
            <div class="stat-card">
                <span class="stat-value">91,505</span>
                <span class="stat-label">Targets Scanned</span>
            </div>
        </div>

        <h3>The Attack Chain</h3>

        <p>The PCPcat operation leveraged two critical vulnerabilities in combination:</p>

        <div class="cve-card">
            <div class="cve-id">CVE-2025-29927 <span class="cvss-score">Critical</span></div>
            <p style="margin-top: 1rem; margin-bottom: 0;">Next.js middleware authorization bypass allowing
                attackers to access protected routes and server-side functions without authentication.</p>
        </div>

        <div class="cve-card">
            <div class="cve-id">CVE-2025-66478 <span class="cvss-score">Critical</span></div>
            <p style="margin-top: 1rem; margin-bottom: 0;">Prototype pollution vulnerability in JSON payload
                processing enabling remote code execution via <code>child_process.execSync()</code>.</p>
        </div>

        <h3>How It Worked</h3>

        <ol>
            <li><strong>Mass Scanning:</strong> Attackers used automated scanners to identify public Next.js
                deployments across the internet</li>
            <li><strong>Fingerprinting:</strong> Applications were fingerprinted to identify vulnerable versions
            </li>
            <li><strong>Malware Delivery:</strong> The <code>react.py</code> malware was distributed to compromised
                hosts</li>
            <li><strong>Prototype Pollution:</strong> Malicious JSON payloads exploited CVE-2025-66478 to achieve
                code execution</li>
            <li><strong>RCE Confirmation:</strong> Attackers confirmed RCE with an <code>id</code> command test</li>
            <li><strong>Credential Harvesting:</strong> Systematic extraction of secrets from compromised servers
            </li>
        </ol>

        <h3>What Was Stolen</h3>

        <p>The attackers systematically exfiltrated high-value credentials from every compromised server:</p>

        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Target</th>
                    <th>Location</th>
                    <th>Impact</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td>.env files</td>
                    <td>Project root, /app, /src</td>
                    <td>Database credentials, API keys, secrets</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>SSH Keys</td>
                    <td>~/.ssh/</td>
                    <td>Lateral movement to other servers</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>AWS Configs</td>
                    <td>~/.aws/credentials</td>
                    <td>Full cloud infrastructure access</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Docker Tokens</td>
                    <td>~/.docker/config.json</td>
                    <td>Container registry access, supply chain risk</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Git Credentials</td>
                    <td>~/.git-credentials, .gitconfig</td>
                    <td>Source code access, supply chain attacks</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Bash History</td>
                    <td>~/.bash_history</td>
                    <td>Reconnaissance, additional secrets in commands</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-code"></i> Technical Deep Dive: The react.py Malware</h2>

        <p>The <code>react.py</code> malware distributed during Operation PCPcat is a Python-based credential
            harvester designed specifically for server-side JavaScript environments. Key characteristics include:
        </p>

        <h3>Prototype Pollution Exploit</h3>

        <pre><code>// Malicious JSON payload structure

{ “proto”: { “shell”: “/bin/sh”, “env”: { “NODE_OPTIONS”: “–require /tmp/malicious.js” } }, “constructor”: { “prototype”: { “execSync”: “function(cmd) { … }” } } }

        <p>The attack leverages JavaScript's prototype chain to inject malicious properties that are later accessed
            by the application, ultimately leading to command execution.</p>

        <h3>Credential Extraction Script</h3>

        <pre><code># Simplified react.py credential harvesting logic

import os import subprocess

targets = [ ‘.env’, ‘.env.local’, ‘.env.production’, os.path.expanduser(‘/.ssh/id_rsa’), os.path.expanduser(’/.aws/credentials’), os.path.expanduser(‘/.docker/config.json’), os.path.expanduser(’/.git-credentials’), os.path.expanduser(‘~/.bash_history’) ]

for target in targets: if os.path.exists(target): with open(target, ‘r’) as f: exfiltrate(f.read())

        <h2><i class="fas fa-road"></i> Why This Keeps Happening: The Framework Blindspot</h2>

        <h3>1. The "Frontend" Security Gap</h3>

        <p>Most organizations apply different security standards to "frontend" vs "backend" systems. Next.js
            applications often:</p>

        <ul>
            <li>Don't receive the same security audits as traditional backends</li>
            <li>Are deployed by frontend developers unfamiliar with server security</li>
            <li>Run in shared or less-secured infrastructure</li>
            <li>Have lax secret management because "it's just the frontend"</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>2. The .env Credential Dump Problem</h3>

        <p>Next.js applications commonly store production secrets in <code>.env</code> files for convenience:</p>

        <pre><code># Typical .env file in compromised Next.js apps

DATABASE_URL=postgresql://prod-user:SuperSecret123@prod-db.internal:5432/main AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=sk_live_51… GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL=https://hooks.slack.com/services/…

        <p>When attackers achieve RCE, this single file provides access to:</p>
        <ul>
            <li>Production databases</li>
            <li>Cloud infrastructure (AWS, GCP, Azure)</li>
            <li>Payment processing (Stripe, etc.)</li>
            <li>Internal communications (Slack)</li>
            <li>Source code repositories (GitHub/GitLab tokens)</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>3. The "Build vs Runtime" Confusion</h3>

        <p>Developers often don't understand the difference between build-time and runtime environment variables in
            Next.js. Secrets meant only for builds end up accessible at runtime, expanding the attack surface.</p>

        <blockquote>
            "We put the AWS keys in .env.local because we thought they were only used during deployment. We didn't
            realize the running server could access them too."
            <cite>— Anonymous victim organization</cite>
        </blockquote>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-history"></i> Timeline of Operation PCPcat</h2>

        <div class="timeline">
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">December 2025 - Day 0</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">Attackers begin mass internet scanning for Next.js deployments.
                    Fingerprinting begins to identify vulnerable versions.</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">Day 0 + 12 Hours</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">First wave of exploitation begins. CVE-2025-29927 used to bypass
                    authentication on targeted applications.</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">Day 0 + 18 Hours</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">react.py malware distributed to compromised hosts. Prototype pollution
                    exploits (CVE-2025-66478) achieve RCE.</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">Day 0 + 24 Hours</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">Over 30,000 servers compromised. Credential exfiltration at scale
                    begins.</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">Day 0 + 48 Hours</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">Campaign reaches peak. 59,128 servers compromised out of 91,505 scanned
                    (64.6% success rate).</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">December 2025</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">Security researchers identify campaign. Public disclosure begins.
                    Organizations scramble to assess exposure.</span>
            </div>
        </div>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-shield-alt"></i> Immediate Response Actions</h2>

        <div class="success-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> If You Run Next.js or React SSR:</strong>
            <ol style="margin-top: 1rem; margin-bottom: 0;">
                <li><strong>Patch Immediately:</strong> Update Next.js to the latest patched version</li>
                <li><strong>Assume Compromise:</strong> If you were running vulnerable versions, assume credentials
                    were stolen</li>
                <li><strong>Rotate ALL Secrets:</strong> Every credential in your .env files must be rotated</li>
                <li><strong>Review AWS Activity:</strong> Check CloudTrail for unauthorized access using stolen keys
                </li>
                <li><strong>Check SSH Keys:</strong> Audit authorized_keys on all connected servers</li>
                <li><strong>Review Git History:</strong> Look for unauthorized commits or repository access</li>
            </ol>
        </div>

        <h3>Checking Your Exposure</h3>

        <pre><code># Check Next.js version

cat package.json | grep next

Search for sensitive files that may have been accessed

        <h3>Secret Rotation Checklist</h3>

        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Secret Type</th>
                    <th>Location</th>
                    <th>Action</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td>Database passwords</td>
                    <td>.env, .env.local</td>
                    <td>Rotate in DB, update .env</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>AWS Access Keys</td>
                    <td>.env, ~/.aws/credentials</td>
                    <td>Deactivate in IAM, create new keys</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>API Keys</td>
                    <td>.env</td>
                    <td>Regenerate in each service dashboard</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>SSH Keys</td>
                    <td>~/.ssh/</td>
                    <td>Generate new keypairs, remove old from authorized_keys</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>GitHub/GitLab Tokens</td>
                    <td>.env, ~/.git-credentials</td>
                    <td>Revoke in developer settings, create new PATs</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-search"></i> Indicators of Compromise (IoCs)</h2>

        <h3>Files to Look For</h3>
        <ul>
            <li><code>/tmp/react.py</code> or variations</li>
            <li>Unexplained Python scripts in temp directories</li>
            <li>Modified <code>.bashrc</code> or <code>.profile</code> files</li>
            <li>New cron jobs or scheduled tasks</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Network Indicators</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>Outbound connections to unfamiliar IPs on ports 443, 8443, 9999</li>
            <li>Large data transfers (credential dumps)</li>
            <li>C2 beaconing patterns</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>SIEM Detection Query (Splunk)</h3>

| search (uri_path=“proto” OR uri_path=“constructor” OR uri_path=“.env”) | stats count by src_ip, uri_path, status | where count > 10

        <h2><i class="fas fa-lock"></i> Long-Term Security Recommendations</h2>

        <h3>1. Treat Next.js Like a Backend</h3>
        <p>Apply the same security controls you would to any Node.js server:</p>
        <ul>
            <li>Regular security audits and penetration testing</li>
            <li>Hardened container images</li>
            <li>Network segmentation</li>
            <li>Runtime application self-protection (RASP)</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>2. Migrate Away from .env Files</h3>
        <p>Use proper secret management solutions:</p>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>AWS Secrets Manager</strong> or <strong>HashiCorp Vault</strong></li>
            <li><strong>Environment-specific injection</strong> rather than file-based storage</li>
            <li><strong>Runtime secret fetching</strong> instead of build-time embedding</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>3. Implement Least Privilege</h3>
        <p>Your Next.js application probably doesn't need:</p>
        <ul>
            <li>Full AWS admin access</li>
            <li>Write access to production databases</li>
            <li>SSH keys to other infrastructure</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>4. Monitor for Framework Vulnerabilities</h3>
        <p>Subscribe to security advisories for:</p>
        <ul>
            <li>Next.js: <a href="https://github.com/vercel/next.js/security/advisories"
                    style="color: var(--accent-cyan);">GitHub Security Advisories</a></li>
            <li>React: Official security announcements</li>
            <li>Node.js: Node.js Security Working Group</li>
        </ul>

                </li>
